Issued at 139 AM MDT Mon Jul 20 2026

It finally fairly quiet on a night shift, with only very isolated 
showers over Johnson County and the Wind River as I write this. 
These should be gone over the next couple of hours. And for the most 
part, the morning should be dry.

We two issues to deal with this afternoon. The first is the one we 
have been talking about ad nauseam for the past five days, the 
monsoonal moisture and the potential for convection. For the most 
part, the deepest moisture will remain south of the area over the 
next 24 hours. This, plus some warmer air at the mid levels
should help cap the atmosphere somewhat. This should keep 
shower and thunderstorm coverage fairly sparse. Precipitable 
water values remain rather high though, generally about 150 
percent of normal, approaching 180 percent in Sweetwater County.
This is where the best chance of convection will be, but even 
here it is only around a 1 in 4 chance for the most part. As for
heavy rain and potential flooding, the Excessive Rainfall 
Outlook is still out of the area. I could see a few heavier 
storms here and the chance of flooding is not zero. However, 
since the storms would be isolated and this area has seen little
rain since the monsoon started, the chance is low. The moisture
deepens later at night, but with the instability limited this 
would likely only be showers. 

The second issue is the heat. There are a few locations that have 
had the warmest string of high temperatures in station history over 
the 9 days (since last weekends heat wave began). And, we will have 
one more hot day today. High temperatures look similar to yesterday. 
with the warmer spots in the Bighorn Basin, like Worland and 
Greybull, having a 1 in 2 chance of highs of 100 or higher. 
Elsewhere, like yesterday, highs in the 90s will be almost certain 
in locations below 6200 feet, with 80s in the rest of the populated 
areas.

The monsoon really makes it self felt starting on Tuesday. 
Precipitable water levels return to levels similar to much of late 
last week, generally about 175 to 200 percent of normal. The one 
thing that is missing is some kind of a forcing mechanism, like a 
jet streak or a shortwave. So, these storms look like more of the 
random pop up variety. There will be a better chance of flooding 
with the higher precipitable water content and expected slow 
movement. If there is one good thing, it that much of the area has 
been largely dry the past 48 hours or so, so the soil won't be as 
saturated. Nevertheless, the marginal risk of Excessive Rainfall 
looks justified at this time. The most numerous storms will be in 
western Wyoming on this day, with less coverage north and east. And 
with more cloud cover, temperatures will finally cool off somewhat, 
an average of about 5 degrees when compared to Monday. Showers and 
storms should decrease after sunset, although some will linger 
through the night.

The main event still looks to be on Wednesday. The deepest moisture 
moves over the area during the afternoon and evening. The models 
continue to show a possible record breaking precipitable water 
value, over 1.50 inches, breaking the old record of 1.42 inches. In 
addition, a shortwave will be passing through the area, bringing 
additional lift and an increased coverage of thunderstorms. If there 
is one thing working against flooding, it is that with the 
shortwave, there should be more steering flow and this may mean more 
movement with the thunderstorms. However, the threat of flooding is 
there. The Excessive Rainfall Outlook continues to show a slight 
risk across much of the area, the area has basically not moved since 
yesterday. And, with the shortwave, shows and storms may continue 
well into the evening and even the overnight hours. We will likely 
need a flood watch, possibly as early as Tuesday  afternoon but we 
will let future shifts may this decision. 

Thursday also looks like a rather active day as high precipitable 
waters remain, although about 10 to 20 percent less than Wednesday. 
Nevertheless, this is still 200 percent of average for many 
locations. So, expect another of fairly widespread showers and 
thunderstorms across the area. Following that, somewhat drier air 
will begin to push into the area from the north and west, bring an 
end to the widespread showers and thunderstorms. There will be some 
around each day into next weekend, but more scattered and more 
limited to the favored locations like the mountains. However, above 
normal precipitable waters will linger into the weekend, although 
more on the 125 to 150 percent of normal. And with less cloud cover, 
temperatures should return to above normal levels Friday and 
continue into next weekend, with some triple digit highs possible 
once again in the warmer spots.
